items.title: The refresh path forgets the blocked flag
items.body:
The key is right. Lines 205-207 load the `User` for the token, but nothing reads `user.IsBlocked` before new tokens are issued. The authorize path checks it (`"User is blocked."`, line 39), and login checks it too (throwing "Account is temporarily locked."), so the refresh path is the odd one out.

- "User is blocked." exists only on the authorize path, and refresh never reaches any such check.
- Nothing revokes the family for a blocked user here.
- The new access token carries the usual claims.

excerpts.quote: await db.Users.SingleAsync(x => x.Id == existing.UserId, cancellationToken);
Lines 205-207 load the `User` but never look at `IsBlocked`

items.title: Why substring search on users becomes a sequential scan
items.body:
**Key: its leading-wildcard LIKE and LOWER calls defeat any B-tree index.** EF translates `Email.Contains(q)` into `LIKE '%q%'` and `DisplayName.ToLower()` into `LOWER(...)`. Per doc 09, neither expression can use a B-tree index, so every search is a sequential scan of the users table. At 10⁴ users nobody notices; at 10⁶ the admin page times out. The doc's fix ladder: a sargable prefix match (`StartsWith`), then a `pg_trgm` GIN index, then real search.

- *EF filters in memory*: the query is translated to SQL; the cost is in the database.
- *The Email index is used*: neither expression can use a B-tree index.
- *A regex match re-planned per keystroke*: the translation is LIKE, not a regular expression.

excerpts.quote: `LIKE '%q%'` plus `LOWER(...)` — neither can use a B-tree index
Fix ladder: prefix-match (`StartsWith`, sargable) → `pg_trgm` GIN index → real search.

items.title: Core idea: what an authorization code is bound to
items.body:
In the authorization code flow, the provider first gives the application a short-lived code, and the application then trades that code for tokens. The danger is that a code can be copied on the way, for example from a log or through a bad redirect.

While reading stages 1 to 3, make two lists. First, everything the provider stores on the code row when it mints it, and in what form (plain value, hash, expiry, flags). Second, everything the token endpoint compares again at the exchange, and against what. For each comparison, say which attacker it stops and what that attacker would need to know to get past it. The chapter's table names an attack for each line, so check your list against it afterwards. Also note which PKCE methods the code accepts.

excerpts.quote: is a checklist — every line is a distinct attack it forecloses

readMore.why: The AuthorizationCode entity and its IsActive rule.

items.title: Without an audience check, any client's token fits
items.body:
The key is right. The JwtBearer options set `ValidateIssuer = true` but `ValidateAudience = false`, so the API never asks which application the token was minted for. If a token for some other client carries the right permission claims, the admin API accepts it.

- Lifetime is still validated: no `ClockSkew` is set, so JwtBearer's default 5-minute skew applies and tokens fail soon after expiry.
- Issuer is validated, so foreign issuers fail.
- Signature validation stays on, so unsigned tokens fail.

excerpts.quote: ValidateAudience = false,
so a token minted for any client works against the admin API if it carries the right permission claims.

items.title: Why a stolen refresh token works without the client secret
items.body:
**Key: only the public client_id, because omitting the secret skips its check.** The refresh grant validates the client secret only inside `if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(request.ClientSecret))`. A request that sends no secret never enters that block, so for a confidential client the check is skipped rather than failed. Finding F5: a stolen refresh token plus the public client_id is enough. Doc 08 notes the bug was found by comparing the refresh path's secret check with the code path's.

- *The client secret, checked on every refresh*: it is checked only when the request volunteers one.
- *The original code_verifier*: PKCE belongs to the code exchange, and F5 says the refresh token and client_id suffice.
- *A live access token*: nothing on the refresh path asks for one; again, the token and client_id suffice.

excerpts.quote: Secret verified only when the request volunteers one. Stolen refresh token + public client_id suffices.
if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(request.ClientSecret))

items.title: Why a mocked DbContext tells you nothing about the SQL
items.body:
**Key: the SQL translation is part of what the service test must check.** Doc 07's shape mix is mostly service-level tests against a real database (EF Core on PostgreSQL via Testcontainers), a few pure unit tests for crypto helpers and domain methods, and a few WebApplicationFactory tests for the HTTP contract. A mocked `DbSet` evaluates LINQ in memory, so a query the database could never run can still pass: in the doc's words, it lies to you.

- *Pure unit tests with no database*: those are the minority, kept for crypto helpers and domain methods.
- *A mock rejects LINQ that PostgreSQL would translate*: the risk runs the other way; the mock accepts too much.
- *WebApplicationFactory tests already cover every query*: there are only a few, aimed at the HTTP contract.

excerpts.quote: mocked `DbSet` LINQ lies to you; the SQL translation *is* part of what you're testing.
for the HTTP contract (form binding, policies, status codes).

items.title: Logged out of everything: check replay detection first
items.body:
**Key: replay detection fired, so query the audit table for `refresh_token.reuse_detected` first.** Doc 07 ranks the hypotheses by prior probability and runs the cheapest probe first. Replay detection comes first: one SQL query over the audit table, which also tells you the IP. An admin force-logout comes second (`admin.user_force_logout`, audit again), and natural expiry third (compare the `ExpiresAt` values). The audit table answers all three in one query, which is the doc's argument for audit completeness.

- *Natural expiry*: it is the third hypothesis, not the first.
- *Admin force-logout*: it is the second.
- *Key rotation*: it is not one of the three; the doc raises it only because rotation writes no audit event, so a rotation-caused mass logout would be invisible.

excerpts.quote: query audit for `refresh_token.reuse_detected` (one SQL query, also tells you the IP)
The audit table answers all three in one query

items.title: The second redirect check binds code and redirect
items.body:
The key is right. The code row stores the redirect URI used at authorize time, and the exchange compares it with the one presented now (`redirect_uri mismatch.`). That proves the party redeeming the code saw the same redirect the code was issued for, which blocks mix-up attacks.

- Authorize did validate it; this second check binds the code to that same redirect.
- Tokens are returned in the HTTP response to the caller, not posted to the URI.
- Client secrets are checked separately, earlier in the exchange.

excerpts.quote: throw new InvalidOperationException("redirect_uri mismatch.");
it proves the exchanger saw the same redirect the code was issued for

items.title: The plain method removes the hash
items.body:
The key is right. In the exchange switch, `"plain" => request.CodeVerifier`: the expected challenge is the verifier itself. So the value sent at authorize time is the same secret needed at exchange time, and anyone who saw the first request can redeem the code.

- The redirect comparison runs for every method.
- Code lifetime is fixed at 5 minutes whatever the method.
- The audit entry for an issued code records the app name and scope, not the challenge.

excerpts.quote: "plain" => request.CodeVerifier,
with `plain`, stealing the challenge *is* stealing the verifier.

items.title: A dead token showing up revokes the whole family
items.body:
The key is right. RT1 has `ReplacedById` set, so `IsActive` is false. The service calls `RevokeFamilyForReuseAsync`, which loads every token with the same `FamilyId`, calls `MarkReuse` on each (reuse time and revoked time), and writes `refresh_token.reuse_detected`.

- The server cannot tell thief from victim, so it does not keep RT2 alive.
- An inactive token is never accepted again.
- No new child is minted on reuse; the request fails.

excerpts.quote: item.MarkReuse(clock.UtcNow);
RT1,RT2,RT3 all marked reused+revoked

items.title: Start here: an identity provider you can read end to end
items.body:
dotnet-auth (NetAuth0) is a small Auth0-style identity provider in .NET: it logs users in and hands applications tokens. The `docs2/` folder is a course; this quest uses chapter 03, "OAuth2 & OIDC, Learned From This Code", which explains each idea with a link to the exact lines that implement it.

Read it in its five stages: the authorization request, PKCE, the token exchange, refresh token rotation, and signing keys. For each stage, open `OAuthService.cs` at the linked lines before reading on. Most of the security rules are one `if` statement each, so you can see exactly where a check happens and what would break without it.

The chapter also lists the repo's known weak spots; treat them as review practice, not as a recipe.

excerpts.quote: explain OAuth2/OIDC, PKCE, JWTs, refresh rotation, and key rotation **with code citations instead of definitions**.

readMore.why: The course overview and how the projects fit together.

items.title: Codes are stored as hashes with a short life
items.body:
The key is right. The service mints `secrets.UrlSafe(32)` and stores `secrets.Sha256Base64Url(code)` with an expiry of `clock.UtcNow.AddMinutes(5)`. `AuthorizationCode.IsActive` requires `ConsumedAt is null && ExpiresAt > now`, so a code works once and only briefly.

- The plain code is never stored, only its hash.
- BCrypt is used for passwords and client secrets, which can be low-entropy; a 32-byte random code needs only a fast hash.
- Codes are random strings, not JWTs.

excerpts.quote: clock.UtcNow.AddMinutes(5)
public bool IsActive(DateTimeOffset now) => ConsumedAt is null && ExpiresAt > now;

items.title: Put the regression test where the bug lived
items.body:
**Key: at the layer where the bug lived, not the layer it surfaced in.** Doc 07's playbook ends every investigation the same way: reproduce, bisect the layer, test one hypothesis with the cheapest probe, find the root cause, then write a regression test. A drifted permission string shows up as a 403 in the admin UI, but the defect lives where the claim and policy strings are defined, so that is where the test goes. It should fail before the fix and pass after.

- *Where it surfaced*: the doc says explicitly not there.
- *One end-to-end UI test*: that tests the surface, not the layer the bug lived in.
- *One test per layer it crossed*: the playbook asks for one regression test, at the root cause's layer.

excerpts.quote: write the regression test at the layer the bug lived in, not the layer it surfaced in.
bisect the layer → one hypothesis → cheapest probe

items.title: PKCE ties the code to a secret the app never sent
items.body:
The key is right. At authorize time the app sends only `code_challenge` (with S256, `SHA256(verifier)`), stored on the code row. At exchange time it must present the raw verifier; the server hashes it (or, for plain, uses it as is) and compares with `FixedTimeEquals`. An attacker with the code but not the verifier fails "PKCE verification failed."

- Codes are not bound to IP addresses.
- Codes are random strings, not encrypted with a client secret; a SPA has no secret.
- The token endpoint never asks for the user's password.

excerpts.quote: throw new InvalidOperationException("PKCE verification failed.");
still can't redeem it without the verifier, which never left the legitimate client.

items.title: Beyond the protocol: reviewing, testing and operating the provider
items.body:
The later quizzes and flashcards in this pack leave chapter 03 behind and use four other parts of the `docs2/` course. They are about the work around the protocol: auditing it, testing it, debugging it and running it.

1. **Chapter 08, the security review walkthrough.** A review method, then a table of findings F1 to F17 with evidence links, a note on which part of the method caught each one, and a list of fixes. For each row, open the evidence link and confirm the claim in the code before you read the next one.
2. **Chapter 07, testing and debugging.** Where tests belong in this repo and how CI is set up, which abstractions make the code testable, and a debugging playbook with two worked scenarios. Before each scenario, write down what you would check, then compare.
3. **Chapter 09, performance and operations.** Rough costs of the expensive operations and the queries that will get slower as data grows. For each query it flags, guess why it will slow down before you read on.
4. **The end of chapter 04**, a short list of promises the flows are meant to keep, with notes on which ones the code really keeps.

excerpts.quote: the findings double as the repo's risk register.
debug systematically instead of by vibes.

readMore.why: The review method, the findings table and the fixes.
Test strategy, worked test examples and the debugging playbook.
Unit costs, queries that age badly, observability and runbooks.

items.title: Why rotating IP addresses beats a per-IP rate limiter
items.body:
**Key: an attacker rotating source IPs, since each address gets its own bucket.** The `public-auth` policy builds a fixed-window limiter (20 per minute, no queue) partitioned on `context.Connection.RemoteIpAddress`. With no proxy in front, that is the attacker's own address, so every new address starts a fresh window. Behind a proxy the opposite failure appears: everyone shares the proxy's single bucket. Finding F12 rates it deployment-dependent, and the fix list pairs `ForwardedHeaders` with a smarter partition key.

- *A forged X-Forwarded-For header*: no forwarded-headers configuration exists, so the header is never read.
- *Varying the email*: the partition key is the connection address, not the account.
- *Switching client_id*: the client plays no part in the key either.

excerpts.quote: without one, attacker IP rotation defeats it. No forwarded-headers config exists.
context.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString() ?? "unknown",

items.title: Core idea: long-lived secrets need extra care
items.body:
Access tokens here live for minutes, but refresh tokens live for days, so a stolen refresh token is a stolen session. Signing keys also live long, and replacing one affects every token already signed with it.

Read stage 4 and trace `ExchangeRefreshTokenAsync` line by line. Note what happens to the presented token on a normal use, which fields link tokens to each other, and how the code treats a token that was already rotated, a token that has expired, and a token whose user has since been blocked. Write down the order of those checks.

Then read stage 5 and the JWKS endpoint. Note which keys the server publishes after a rotation and for how long, and what the API's JwtBearer settings do and do not validate.

excerpts.quote: A stolen one is a stolen session.

readMore.why: Signing, JWKS publication and the current key.

items.title: An MFA enrollment found by its ID and nothing else
items.body:
**Key: by enrollment ID alone, without comparing the caller to its owner.** `VerifyTotpEnrollmentAsync` loads the enrollment with `x.Id == request.EnrollmentId` and then checks the TOTP code. It never asks who is calling, so anyone who knows another user's enrollment ID and a valid code for it can verify that enrollment. Finding F8 calls it part of a pattern of unscoped lookups, and the fix list pairs it with F2: take user and tenant scope from claims and look rows up by compound keys (the `Id` plus the owner).

- *ID plus the user ID from the token*: that compound lookup is the fix, not today's code.
- *The caller's own pending enrollment*: the query has no user filter.
- *ID within the caller's tenant*: no tenant from the claims takes part either.

excerpts.quote: Verification looks up by enrollment ID only; caller's identity never checked.
var enrollment = await db.MfaEnrollments.SingleAsync(x => x.Id == request.EnrollmentId, cancellationToken);
change service lookups to compound keys

items.title: Retired keys stay published for a week
items.body:
The key is right. `GetJwksAsync` returns keys where `RetiredAt == null || RetiredAt > clock.UtcNow.AddDays(-7)`. Rotation retires the old key; it is still in the JWKS, and the token's `kid` header selects it, so the signature verifies.

- No restart is needed for rotation.
- JwtBearer always validates the signature.
- Rotation creates a fresh RSA-2048 key; it is not derived from the old one.

excerpts.quote: .Where(x => x.RetiredAt == null || x.RetiredAt > clock.UtcNow.AddDays(-7))
A verifier that fetched JWKS and found only the new `kid` would reject *valid* tokens.

items.title: Expiry is checked before reuse
items.body:
The key is right. The first test after loading is `if (existing.ExpiresAt <= clock.UtcNow)`: the token is revoked, saved, and the call fails with "Refresh token expired." The reuse check comes after, so it never runs for an expired token.

- No family revocation or reuse audit happens on this path.
- Expiry is checked; it is the very first check.
- This method never blocks or locks a user.

excerpts.quote: throw new InvalidOperationException("Refresh token expired.");
an *expired* token is revoked quietly without family revocation.

items.title: Redirect URIs must match exactly
items.body:
The key is right. `ValidateRedirectUri` accepts a request only if some registered URI satisfies `string.Equals(x.Uri, redirectUri, StringComparison.Ordinal)`. `/cb/extra` is a different string, so it throws "redirect_uri is not registered."

- Prefix matching is the classic OAuth hole the chapter warns about.
- Matching the host is not enough; the whole string is compared.
- The rule is the same for every client type.

excerpts.quote: string.Equals(x.Uri, redirectUri, StringComparison.Ordinal)
This single check is what stops an attacker from receiving your authorization code

items.title: Recovery codes that nothing ever redeems
items.body:
**Key: they stay locked out, because no login path ever redeems a recovery code.** Enrollment generates ten recovery codes, stores their SHA-256 hashes and shows them to the user once. Nothing consumes them: `RecoveryCode.Use` has no callers, and the login MFA branch verifies only a TOTP code. Finding F6 calls the codes decorative: a lost authenticator means permanent lockout, while the API advertises recovery. Doc 08 puts it under the negative-space pass, because you only find it by asking what code *should* exist.

- *Log in once with a code, then MFA resets*: no code path accepts a recovery code at all.
- *Redeem after an admin unblocks the account*: unblocking does not create a redemption path.
- *Enter a code instead of the TOTP and it is consumed*: that is exactly the missing feature; the fix list calls adding it feature completion.

excerpts.quote: Generated and stored; no redemption path exists. Lost authenticator = permanent lockout, while the API advertises recovery.
db.RecoveryCodes.Add(new RecoveryCode(userId, secrets.Sha256Base64Url(code)));

items.title: Why there is no implicit flow
items.body:
The key is right. The first check in `CreateAuthorizationCodeAsync` refuses anything but `response_type=code`. The old implicit flow returned tokens inside the URL fragment of the redirect, where browser history and Referer headers can leak them. The code flow returns only a short-lived code.

- PKCE is a code-flow feature; it is not why other types are refused.
- Speed plays no part in the reasoning.
- Discovery documents can list several response types; the restriction is a choice.

excerpts.quote: throw new InvalidOperationException("Only response_type=code is supported.");
it returned tokens in URL fragments where they leak via browser history and Referer headers.

items.title: Why every token-endpoint error looks the same to a client
items.body:
**Key: every failure becomes a generic 400 that is not shaped per RFC 6749.** The API has one exception handler, and it answers every unhandled exception with a problem response titled "Request failed" and status 400; in Development it also copies the exception message into the detail. OAuth client libraries expect RFC 6749 error bodies such as `invalid_grant` or `invalid_client`, so here they cannot tell one failure from another (finding F10). The fix list proposes a small exception hierarchy with a mapped handler, so token errors become spec-shaped and unexpected errors become 500s.

- *Both return 401 with different WWW-Authenticate headers*: the handler always sends 400.
- *Both become a 500*: 500s are what the fix would introduce for unexpected errors; today everything is 400.
- *Spec-shaped errors with the field stripped in production*: the errors are never RFC 6749-shaped in any environment.

excerpts.quote: OAuth errors are not RFC 6749-shaped, so client libraries can't distinguish
statusCode: StatusCodes.Status400BadRequest);
token errors become spec-shaped and unexpected errors become 500s.

items.title: Same message, different latency: the login timing oracle
items.body:
**Key: unknown users skip the BCrypt verify, so their failures return faster.** `LoginAsync` throws "Invalid credentials." as soon as the user lookup finds nothing, before any password work. For a real account with a wrong password it first runs the BCrypt verify (work factor 12, hundreds of milliseconds) and then throws the same message. The text is uniform but the latency is not, so timing reveals which emails have accounts (finding F11).

- *A different message once the tenant slug is valid*: both paths throw the identical "Invalid credentials." text.
- *BCrypt runs twice for unknown users*: it does not run at all for them.
- *Slower only after the account locks*: a locked account gets its own message before any password check, so no BCrypt runs there either.

excerpts.quote: Unknown-user login skips the BCrypt verify (work factor 12, hundreds of ms); uniform message, non-uniform latency.
?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Invalid credentials.");

items.title: Asymmetric signing keeps the signing key in one place
items.body:
The key is right. HS256 uses one shared secret for signing and verifying, so every API that verifies tokens could also create them. With RS256 the provider signs with a private key and publishes only the public part, so resource servers can verify but not forge.

- HS256 tokens can carry a `kid` too; rotation is not the issue.
- Size and cost are not the chapter's argument.
- JwtBearer supports HS256; the choice is about trust.

excerpts.quote: HS256 is symmetric — every verifier holds the *signing* key, so any resource server could forge tokens.

items.title: Single-use holds only one request at a time
items.body:
The key is right. Both requests load the row while `ConsumedAt` is still null, so both pass `IsActive`. `code.Consume(...)` only changes memory and is saved later. The `AuthorizationCode` mapping has a unique index on `CodeHash` but no concurrency token, so the second save does not fail.

- No 409 can come from EF without a concurrency token.
- Neither read waits: on Postgres a plain SELECT takes no row lock, and the code asks for none.
- ConsumedAt is set after validation, near the end.

excerpts.quote: code.Consume(clock.UtcNow);
so two requests that load the same unconsumed code at the same moment both pass line 123 and both get tokens.

items.title: A test that no pipeline runs protects nothing
items.body:
**Key: CI runs only the UnitTests project, so a CI step must be added.** The workflow has exactly one test command, `dotnet test tests/NetAuth0.UnitTests/NetAuth0.UnitTests.csproj`. NetAuth0.IntegrationTests already references the Api project, `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing` and `Testcontainers.PostgreSql`, but it has no `.cs` files and no CI step. Tests you add there run only on your machine until someone adds that step; in doc 07's words, a test that no pipeline runs is documentation, not protection.

- *Testcontainers cannot start Docker on ubuntu-latest*: the doc says those runners have Docker.
- *The project lacks the packages*: it already has both of them.
- *CI runs every project but skips Docker tests*: CI runs one project only.

excerpts.quote: a test that no pipeline runs is documentation, not protection.
That step needs Docker on the runner (Testcontainers); `ubuntu-latest` GitHub runners have it.
dotnet test tests/NetAuth0.UnitTests/NetAuth0.UnitTests.csproj

items.title: 401 or 403: the question that halves the search
items.body:
**Key: ask whether it is 401 or 403, since that splits authentication from authorization.** In doc 07's worked scenario, a 401 means authentication failed: the token is absent or invalid. A 403 means authorization failed: the token is valid but a claim is missing. Answering that one question halves the search space before any other probe runs. A senior also remembers that this repo's catch-all 400 can mask both.

- *Is the JWT expired*: expiry is checked on the 401 branch, in step 3, after the first question.
- *Is the user's role seeded*: empty permissions are checked on the 403 branch, in step 4.
- *Is the API reachable*: the scenario starts from a failing status code; the first move is to read which one it is.

excerpts.quote: 401 = authentication (token absent/invalid), 403 = authorization (valid token, missing claim). This one question halves the search space.

items.title: Why TOTP guessing is limited only by the IP rate limiter
items.body:
**Key: only the per-IP limiter, since failed codes never count toward lockout.** In `LoginAsync`, a wrong password calls `RegisterFailure`, which drives lockout. A wrong TOTP code takes a different branch: it writes an `mfa.failure` audit event and throws, without touching the failure counter. The verifier also discards the matched time step (`out _`), so a code is never rejected for being reused. Finding F3 concludes that only the per-IP limiter of 20 requests a minute protects the space of 10⁶ codes.

- *A lockout after repeated bad codes*: that is the password branch; MFA failures bypass it.
- *A per-account counter that slows each attempt*: there is no per-account counter at all.
- *Nothing, since the limiter skips MFA*: the finding names the per-IP limiter as the one remaining guard.

excerpts.quote: MFA failures bypass `RegisterFailure`; no per-account counter, no per-step replay rejection
throw new InvalidOperationException("Invalid MFA code.");

items.title: Why the review starts at trust boundaries and ends in negative space
items.body:
**Key: trust boundaries need no domain knowledge; negative space needs all of it.** Doc 08 orders its four passes by how much you must understand about the system. Asking which inputs the server trusts works on an endpoint you have never seen before. Asking what is *missing* (an audit event nobody writes, recovery codes nobody redeems) only works once you know what should be there.

- *Trust-boundary bugs are always the most severe*: the doc ties the order to knowledge, and it says elsewhere that severity depends on context.
- *Negative space is the cheapest pass*: the doc calls it the hardest, because you are searching for what is not there.
- *The asset pass needs the trust pass's endpoint list*: no hand-off between passes is described; each pass asks its own question.

excerpts.quote: trust boundaries first because they require zero domain knowledge, negative space last because it requires all of it.
The hardest pass, because you're grepping for what isn't there.
